analysis.one_liner: Ends a special tax-rate cut for domestic oil and gas producers and refiners.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007, without a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2004 Congress replaced a repealed export tax break with a lower effective tax rate for domestic manufacturers — and made oil and gas companies eligible even though they had never qualified for the original export break. With oil prices and industry profits surging in 2006, this bill would amend the tax code so income from producing, refining, transporting, or distributing oil and natural gas no longer qualifies for that rate cut. Oil companies would go back to paying the standard corporate rate on those earnings.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, in the form of a more level tax code and federal revenue that would otherwise be spent as a tax cut on some of the most profitable companies in the country during an oil price spike. The bill's own findings called the existing arrangement a 'reverse windfall profits tax' that lowered the tax rate on the industry's windfall profits [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Denies the 2004 domestic-manufacturing tax deduction (Section 199) for income from the production, refining, processing, transportation, or distribution of oil, natural gas, or their primary products, raising the effective tax rate on those earnings [S2] [S3].

The bill's findings argue oil and gas producers were made eligible for the rate reduction even though they suffered no detriment from repeal of the old export-related tax provisions, and that the benefit acted as a 'reverse windfall profits tax' on their windfall profits [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and natural gas producers, refiners, and related companies, which would lose the reduced effective tax rate on domestic production income beginning with tax years after 2005 [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The industry and its allies argued the manufacturing rate cut supports domestic energy production, and that raising taxes on producers amid high prices could discourage investment in domestic supply — a cost that could surface later at the pump [S3].

The bill was drafted as a one-line amendment with no revenue estimates or transition provisions, so its actual revenue effect and any disruption to existing industry tax planning were never analyzed in committee [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core policy is straightforward tax fairness: it removes a rate break for companies that were never meant to have it, during a period of record profits. The honest counterweight is that higher taxes on domestic producers can feed into energy costs, and the bill was never refined or scored, so those trade-offs were never weighed in public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2006 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007 [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Kerry introduced the bill on April 27, 2006, with Sen. Reid introducing it on his behalf; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S3] [S5].
No further action was taken — no committee markup, no floor vote — and the bill expired with the Congress on January 3, 2007 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies, which kept the reduced effective tax rate on domestic production income that the bill would have ended, including through the 2006 price spike the bill's findings described as windfall profits. Nobody is better off because of what happened except the industry and its shareholders.

for.name: Sen. John Kerry
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and gave introductory remarks on April 27, 2006.

for.name: Sen. Harry Reid
for.role: U.S. Senator from Nevada and Senate Minority Leader
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on Sen. Kerry's behalf.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Senate committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on April 27, 2006 and took no further action — no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no one else joined as a cosponsor, so the partisan shape of any potential vote was never tested [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Oil and natural gas producers and refiners
industries.note: The bill would remove their eligibility for the Section 199 domestic-manufacturing tax deduction, effectively raising their tax rate on domestic oil and gas income to the standard corporate level. Its interest ran against the bill's tax-fairness aim for ordinary taxpayers.
